notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Deuteronomy 33, drawn entirely from the sources I was able to access. I note where denominational or other distinctive views could not be found due to search limits.

---

## Deuteronomy 33 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

The chapter records Moses' final blessing upon the tribes of Israel before his death, deliberately modeled after Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49. Unlike Jacob's blessing, which mingled prophecy with rebuke, Moses gives only blessings. The tribe of Simeon is omitted, likely because they were absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:9).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

The Pulpit Commentary notes that this blessing was probably spoken on the same day as the Song of Moses (Deut. 32). "In the song, Moses dwells chiefly on the calamities that were to befall the people because of their apostasy; in the blessing, he depicts the benefits that were to be enjoyed by them through the Divine favor."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 1 — "This is the blessing that Moses the man of God pronounced…"

**"Man of God."** This title is used of Moses here for the first time in the Pentateuch (the second occurrence is Joshua 14:6, also of Moses). Later it became a designation for prophets (e.g., Elijah, Elisha; Judges 13:6; 1 Sam. 9:6). Ellicott observes: "The more any man is a 'servant to Jehovah,' the more is he a 'man of Elohim' to his fellow-men." Gill adds that Moses is called this "being raised up of God, and eminently qualified by him…inspired by a spirit of prophecy." Rashi commented, "And if not then, when should he bless them?" — meaning that just before death was the fitting time.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html (Ellicott)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm (Gill)
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary (Precept Austin, quoting JFB, Maxwell, Wiersbe)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/

The chapter may have been recorded by an editor such as Joshua or Eleazar, since Moses speaks of himself in the third person and refers to his own death (Kalland, cited by Guzik).

---

### v. 2 — "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir…"

**God's appearing as a sunrise.** Ellicott describes the appearance of God at Sinai as a sunrise: "His light rose from Sinai, and the tops of the hills of Seir caught its rays. The full blaze of light shone on Paran." The verbs *came*, *dawned*, and *shone forth* indicate that God's coming was "like the sun flooding the desert area bounded by Sinai on the south, Seir on the northeast, and Paran on the north" (Kalland, cited in Enduring Word).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/

**"With myriads of holy ones."** Gill interprets these as "holy angels," confirmed by the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, Stephen in Acts 7:53, and Paul in Galatians 3:19 — the Law was given through the mediation of angels. This added grandeur and solemnity. Ellicott translates "from the ten thousands of holiness" (not "with"), arguing that the preposition is "from" and the fiery law came *from* the angelic hosts at God's right hand.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

**"Flaming fire at His right hand" (BSB) / "a fiery law" (KJV).** JFB explains: "so called both because of the thunder and lightning which accompanied its promulgation (Ex 19:16-18; Deut 4:11), and the fierce, unrelenting curse denounced against the violation of its precepts (2 Cor 3:7-9)." Gill adds that the law "pierces and penetrates like fire, and works a sense of wrath and fiery indignation…it being the ministration of condemnation and death."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm

Ellicott's additional note discusses the Hebrew word *eshdath*, noting that *dath* (law) is likely a Persian/Chaldean word and that the LXX renders it "angels" instead. He concludes the traditional "fiery law" yields good sense.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 3 — "Surely You love the people…"

**"Surely You love the people."** Maclaren observes that the Hebrew verb form implies "the act spoken about is neither past, present, nor future only, but continuous and perpetual" (cited in Enduring Word). Gill notes this love was a distinguishing blessing shown in giving the law — how much more is God's love shown to His spiritual Israel by giving the Gospel and His Son.

**"All the holy ones are in Your hand."** Gill interprets this of believers who are "in the hands of Christ…preserved in Christ…in His custody and under His protection, and where they are safe from every enemy" (cf. John 10:28). JFB says the reference is to all the tribes of Israel as a holy people.

**"They sit down at Your feet; each receives Your words."** This alludes to the posture of the Israelites at the foot of Mount Sinai receiving the Law (Ex 19:17), and figuratively to disciples sitting at a master's feet (cf. Luke 10:39; Acts 22:3).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

---

### v. 4 — "the law that Moses gave us, the possession of the assembly of Jacob."

Ellicott notes that this verse is "evidently not what Moses said, but an explanatory parenthesis, inserted by the writer, who was probably Joshua." Gill explains that though the Law came from God, it was delivered through Moses, and is called an *inheritance* because "it was to be valued…as a possession, an estate, an inheritance, to be continued among them and transmitted to their posterity" (cf. Ps 119:111).

The Pulpit Commentary homiletics add: "The only real blessing we can confer is to put men into connection with God's channels of blessing… Moses likewise knew that the greatest blessing he could confer on Israel was love of God's Law."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/33.htm

---

### v. 5 — "So the LORD became King in Jeshurun…"

**"King in Jeshurun."** "Jeshurun" means "the upright one" and is a poetical name for Israel (see Deut 32:15). Gill notes a dual interpretation: God was the supreme King (theocracy), and Moses was His vicegerent (chief magistrate). Rashi says, "The Holy One, blessed be He! the yoke of His kingdom is upon them for ever." Ellicott notes Samuel's description of Israel's history as "when the Lord your God was your king" (1 Sam 12:12).

The leaders gathered and tribes assembled refers to the assembly at Sinai to receive the covenant.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/

---

### v. 6 — "Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few."

A modest blessing consistent with Jacob's prophecy that Reuben "shall not excel" (Gen 49:4). As Guzik notes, "no prophet, judge, or king ever came from the tribe of Reuben." Ellicott suggests the threat of extinction came partly from the rebellion of Dathan and Abiram (Reubenites) in Numbers 16 — a terrible destruction that diminished the tribe. Rashi interpreted it spiritually: "'Live' in this world, and 'not die' in the world to come."

Some ancient copies of the LXX insert "Simeon" into this verse ("let Simeon be many in number"), which would fit the tribe's dramatic decline in the wilderness (from 59,300 to 22,200 men).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm

---

### v. 7 — "O LORD, hear the cry of Judah…"

The name Judah means "praise," so Moses prays that the LORD would hear the voice of praise and prayer from Judah. Ellicott calls this "a kingly blessing" and notes that all the prayers of David, Solomon, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Daniel, and ultimately Christ Himself are "the voice of Judah." Moses prays for success in battle and God's help "against his foes." This anticipates Judah's leadership role prophesied in Genesis 49:10 ("the scepter shall not depart from Judah").

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies the difficult phrase about hands: the Hebrew *rab* is not "sufficient" but a participle meaning "he contends," so the sense is "with his hands he contends for his people" — thus needing God's help.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### vv. 8–11 — Levi

**v. 8 — "Give Your Thummim to Levi and Your Urim to Your godly one…"** The Urim and Thummim were the high-priestly stones for discerning God's will (Ex 28:30). Gill sees Christ as the ultimate "Holy One" with the true Urim and Thummim — "lights and perfections." Ellicott sees Aaron, "Moses' own departed brother," as the primary referent, since the people murmured against both Moses and Aaron at Massah and Meribah.

**v. 9 — "He said of his father and mother, 'I do not consider them.'"** This refers to the Levites' loyalty at the golden calf incident (Ex 32:26-29), where they obeyed Moses' call, "Whoever is for the LORD, come to me," and slew even their own "brother, companion, and neighbor" who had fallen into idolatry. Merrill states: "Moses had asked 'whoever is for the Lord' to come forward…Levi volunteered and proceeded to slay their own 'sons and brothers'" (cited in Enduring Word).

**v. 10 — "He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob…"** The tribe of Levi was scattered throughout Israel as teachers (cf. Lev 10:11; 2 Chron 17:9). They also performed the priestly functions of burning incense and offering sacrifices. Gill notes this dual role of teaching and worship.

**v. 11 — "Bless his substance, O LORD…Smash the loins of those who rise against him."** Levi had no land inheritance, living off the tithes of Israel, so a blessing on their "substance" was peculiarly necessary (Clarke, cited by Guzik). Ellicott notes that Rashi saw this fulfilled in the Maccabean wars, where priests (the Hasmoneans) led the deliverance of Israel.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 12 — Benjamin: "May the beloved of the LORD rest secure in Him…"

Jerusalem, the temple city, was in Benjamin's territory. Ellicott translates: "Beloved of Jehovah! He (Jehovah) will dwell in security upon him, covering him over all the day. And between his shoulders (mountain slopes) He hath taken up His abode." Merrill comments: "The anthropomorphism here is suggestive of the most tender compassion and solid security at the same time. The phrase speaks not of carrying on the back but of being held close to the breast or bosom" (cited in Enduring Word). The imagery is of a father carrying a young, tender child (Calvin).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/33-12.htm

---

### vv. 13–17 — Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh)

The longest blessing, corresponding to Joseph receiving the double portion through his two sons.

**v. 13 — "precious dew from heaven…deep waters that lie beneath."** Agricultural blessings with water from above (rain/dew) and below (springs/groundwater). In Palestine, water was crucial for a bountiful harvest.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

**v. 14 — "bountiful harvest from the sun…abundant yield of the seasons."** Ellicott notes these are the "increase of the sun" and the "precious things put forth from month to month" (or by night when the moon rules).

**v. 16 — "the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush."** A blessing unique to Moses. Maclaren reflects: "That was a strange shrine for God, that poor, ragged, dry desert bush…yet it was 'God's house.' Not in the cedars of Lebanon, not in the great monarchs of the forest, but in the forlorn child of the desert did He abide" (cited in Enduring Word). Ellicott adds that from the burning bush Moses "drew the thought that He presented Himself as dwelling in it; and thus he has furnished God's Church with this comfort for all ages, that His human temple, although it burn with fire, can never be consumed."

**"prince of his brothers"** — Hebrew *nazir*, "separated one." Ellicott asks whether this might partly illuminate why Jesus is called a "Nazarene" (Matt 2:23).

**v. 17 — "His majesty is like a firstborn bull…myriads of Ephraim…thousands of Manasseh."** "Like a firstborn bull…or a wild ox, he would rise to ascendancy and exercise dominion (thus thrusting with a horn)" (Merrill, in Enduring Word). Rashi connects the ten thousands slain by Joshua (an Ephraimite) and the thousands slain by Gideon (of Manasseh). The two sons of Joseph are like two horns that push peoples to the ends of the earth.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### vv. 18–19 — Zebulun and Issachar

**v. 18 — "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your journeys, and Issachar, in your tents."** Zebulun was associated with seafaring and trade ("going out"), while Issachar was associated with agriculture and pastoral life ("tents"). Clarke notes: "as Zebulun should be prosperous in his shipping and traffic, so should Issachar be in his tents — his agriculture and pasturage." Both tribes were in the Galilee region.

**v. 19 — "They will call the peoples to a mountain; there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness."** Ellicott interprets: "they shall give the mountain-call to the peoples — i.e., they shall call the tribes of Israel to Mount Moriah to offer the sacrifices of righteousness" (cf. 2 Chron 30:11, 18). Guzik notes the "abundance of the seas" refers to the Sea of Galilee. Merrill observes this has found "startling fulfillment in the modern state of Israel, whose major port is Haifa, located in the area of ancient Zebulun."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### vv. 20–21 — Gad

**v. 20 — "Blessed is he who enlarges the domain of Gad!"** The Gadites had a large inheritance east of the Jordan. "He lies down like a lion and tears off an arm or a head" — Gill notes this figurative language expresses conquering strong and mighty men (the "arm" being strength) and kings and governors (the "crown of the head"). 1 Chronicles 12:8 describes Gadites "whose faces were as the faces of lions."

**v. 21 — "He chose the best land for himself, because a ruler's portion was reserved for him there."** Merrill says: "Gad's area was by far the largest and best, conforming well to its description as 'the leader's portion.'" Gad and the eastern tribes faithfully came with the other tribes ("the leaders of the people") to help conquer Canaan.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/33.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 22 — Dan: "Dan is a lion's cub, leaping out of Bashan."

Guzik notes this may not be entirely complimentary. Jacob compared Dan to a serpent (Gen 49:17). History records Dan as a troublesome tribe: they introduced idolatry (Judges 18:30); Jeroboam set up a golden calf there (1 Kgs 12:26-30). "Leaping from Bashan" prophetically anticipates Dan's migration from the south to the far north (Judges 18). Ellicott calls the taking of Laish "a sudden, treacherous surprise, like the spring of a lion on his prey."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 23 — Naphtali: "abounding with favor, full of the blessing of the LORD…"

Naphtali's territory lay in Galilee near the Sea of Galilee — the very region where Jesus centered His earthly ministry (Matt 4:13-16). Clarke exults: "Scarcely any of the tribes was more particularly favoured…The light of the glorious Gospel of Christ shone brightly here. Christ's chief residence was at Capernaum in this tribe." Jacob had said of Naphtali "he uses beautiful words" (Gen 49:21). The "sea and the south" refer to the Sea of Galilee and the southern regions.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

---

### vv. 24–25 — Asher

**v. 24 — "May Asher be the most blessed of sons…dip his foot in oil."** The region of Asher (the Galilean highlands) was famous for olive oil. Thompson notes that "both Josephus and one of the Jewish Midrashim refer to this fact" (cited in Enduring Word). The abundance is so great one could dip a foot in oil.

**v. 25 — "May the bolts of your gate be iron and bronze, and may your strength match your days."** Ellicott notes that "shoes" (KJV) is better translated "bars" or "fastenings" — the iron and bronze bolts of gates, fitting since Asher's territory was at the northern frontier where invaders would enter. The phrase "as your days, so shall your strength be" is a beloved promise. Clarke says: "Whatever thy trials or difficulties may be, I shall always give thee grace to support thee under and bring thee through them." Spurgeon applied it thus: we receive strength one day at a time, proportionally to our need, in varied forms suited to each day, and constantly as long as our days continue (summarised by Guzik).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

---

### v. 26 — "There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your aid…"

God's greatness is celebrated as the ultimate source of Israel's blessing. Thompson notes the figure of deity riding a chariot through the heavens is an ancient Near Eastern motif also found in Psalm 18:10, 68:33, Isaiah 19:1, and Ezekiel 1. The Pulpit Commentary points out that the Masoretic punctuation directs this to be read "There is none like God, O Jeshurun" — a direct address to Israel.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 27 — "The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms."

The hymn *Leaning on the Everlasting Arms* takes its title from this verse. Guzik expands: "The everlasting arms of God are underneath, as a foundation for everything." Ellicott renders it: "The dwelling of the eternal Jehovah (above thee) / And underneath, the everlasting arms!" — God is both the sheltering roof above and the supporting arms below. "He drives out the enemy before you, giving the command, 'Destroy him!'" reflects the holy-war confidence God gives His people.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 28 — "So Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled…"

The Pulpit Commentary notes the parallelism: "Israel dwelleth securely" parallels "the fountain of Jacob" — Israel is so called because they came forth from Jacob as waters from a copious spring (Ibn Ezra). "A land of grain and new wine, where even the heavens drip with dew" describes Canaan's agricultural richness. Ellicott connects this with the Messianic hope: "In His days (the days of Messiah) Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely" (Jer 23:6).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

### v. 29 — "Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?"

Moses concludes with exultation. God is the "shield" (defense) and "sword" (offensive power) of Israel. The Pulpit Commentary explains: "Thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee; literally, shall feign unto thee; i.e. shall pretend to be thy friends, in order to obtain favor with thee" — fawning with feigned humility (cf. Ps 18:44; 66:2; 81:15). "Trample their high places" means to wholly subdue and triumph over enemies, even capturing their inaccessible mountain strongholds (Rosenmüller).

Guzik notes: "The true greatness of Israel is the same as the greatness of the Christian: not in and of themselves, but in their God." Clarke observed: "'This people shall not be incorporated with any other people under heaven. A prophecy which continues to be fulfilled to the very letter.'"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-33.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

Due to search limits, I was unable to retrieve full content from many tradition-specific sites. However, the following can be noted from the sources accessed:

**Reformed:** The Precept Austin page cites William Kelly, a conservative dispensational writer, who emphasises that Moses' blessing "is altogether in reference to the land which the people were on the point of entering" — stressing the literal, territorial nature of the blessings — and that the closing words "will assuredly be fulfilled in the future brightness and glory of restored Israel." The JFB commentary (Reformed-leaning) interprets the "fiery law" in light of 2 Corinthians 3:7-9 (the law as "ministration of condemnation").
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary

**Baptist:** Spurgeon's applications (cited through Guzik at Enduring Word) on vv. 24-25 emphasise practical, devotional lessons for the believer: the "iron and bronze" sandals represent God's protection of tender feet, strength for difficult paths, power to crush spiritual enemies, and durability for the long journey. His interpretation of "as your days, so shall your strength be" stresses God's daily, proportional, varied, and constant provision of grace.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-33/

**Catholic and Orthodox views** (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org): These could not be accessed within the search limits. No notes available.

**Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org): The NET Bible note (cited in Precept Austin) mentions a textual alternative: "With slight alteration (מִמְרִבַת קָדֵשׁ for the MT's מֵרִבְבֹת קֹדֶשׁ) the translation would be 'from Meribah Kadesh'" — but favours the MT reading of angelic hosts. Ellicott's extended note on *eshdath* discusses the Persian origin of *dath* and the LXX variant, representing older critical scholarship.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-33-commentary
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-33.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic, Lutheran, Methodist, Anglican, and Word of Faith views:** These could not be accessed within the search limits. No notes available.
